value.overview: The Panama Flycatcher (Myiarchus panamensis) is a medium-sized tyrant flycatcher of lowland Central and northern South America. It is associated with dry forest, humid lowland woodland, scrub, clearings, secondary growth, and mangroves. The species often perches upright and launches short flights to capture insects, while also taking small fruits. Costa Rica forms the northern part of its range, where it is a resident of suitable lowland habitats, especially along the Pacific coast.
value.classification: The Panama Flycatcher belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae, and the genus Myiarchus. It is a passerine bird.
value.identification: This is a fairly large, upright Myiarchus flycatcher with a broad bill, slight crest, brown upperparts, a grayish throat, and yellow underparts. The wings and tail are mostly dull brown and lack the strong warm-rufous tones shown by several similar species. Juveniles may show some rufous edging on the wing feathers and tail. Identification is difficult by sight alone, so habitat, range, and voice are useful. Its song consists of clear, separated whistles, sometimes followed by a rapid rolling trill.
value.rangeHabitat: The Panama Flycatcher occurs from Costa Rica through Panama and eastward into Colombia, western Ecuador, and Venezuela. In Costa Rica, it is concentrated in lowland areas, particularly along the Pacific slope from the Gulf of Nicoya south toward the Osa Peninsula; the species also reaches southwestern Costa Rica and occurs in suitable Caribbean lowlands near the Panamanian border. It uses tropical dry and moist forest, forest edges, scrub, clearings, secondary woodland, open areas, and coastal mangroves, generally from sea level to about 1,400 meters.
value.migrationStatus: Generally a year-round resident, including in Costa Rica. Regular long-distance migration is not known, although limited local or elevational movements may occur.
value.breeding: Breeding has been recorded mainly from March through June, with activity possibly continuing into July in some areas. The species nests in tree cavities, usually several meters above the ground, but may also use cavities in buildings or nest boxes. The nest is a bulky lining of rootlets, plant fibers, plant down, animal hair, and sometimes snakeskin. The usual clutch contains two or three eggs. Detailed information on incubation and care of young remains limited.
value.dietFeeding: The Panama Flycatcher feeds mainly on insects and other arthropods, supplemented by small fruits. It commonly waits on an exposed perch and makes short sallies to catch flying prey, often returning to the same perch. It may also pick insects or fruit from foliage. In mangroves and other open coastal habitats, it forages among vegetation and roots and may use low perches close to the ground.
value.behavior: Usually seen alone or in pairs, the Panama Flycatcher is an alert, active bird that often perches upright and scans from the lower or middle levels of vegetation. It defends territories with whistles and other calls, especially around breeding sites. Individuals may forage in scrub, woodland edges, mangroves, and open forest rather than remaining exclusively inside dense forest. Its subdued plumage and habit of sitting quietly can make it easy to overlook.

conservation.populationTrend: The population is considered stable, with a large range and no evidence of a major global decline.
